place: A timber barn with a thatched roof in a showery haymaking season, its bay filled to the tie beams with meadow hay carted a day too early.
things: meadow hay, carted while still tough and a little green
a sweet tobacco smell, later a sharp burnt one
an iron rod pushed into the mow to feel for heat
the cattle tied at the far end
outcome: Hay put up damp ferments and warms itself, and a big tight mow cannot lose the heat. For the first week it smells sweet and steams faintly on cool mornings, which is normal enough to ignore. Over three to six weeks the core goes brown, then black, and the rod comes out too hot to hold. If nobody pulls the mow apart, a carter's load at a time out into the yard, the core chars and then smoulders, and it breaks into open flame when it reaches air, often as someone finally digs into it. The barn, thatch and all, goes in an hour. Even if caught, the heated hay is brown, brittle and poor feed.

place: A cow byre at first light in cold weather, where a newly bought heifer, calved a week ago, stands tied beside the old house cow.

outcome: The old cow stands, lets down her milk at once and gives a gallon and a half in ten minutes to any competent hands. The heifer is another matter: strange person, cold hands, sore udder and a calf calling. She holds her milk up, swishes, and at the second squeeze kicks the pail across the byre and steps in it. With meal in front of her, warmed hands, a quiet voice and the calf where she can see it, she gives perhaps half her milk, fidgeting throughout. The rest stays in her, and a heifer left half-milked for days goes hard in the udder and gives less thereafter.

place: A farmyard in late autumn, pig-killing time, with a stone-flagged cool pantry, a salting trough, and weather that ought to be cold by now but has turned mild and muggy.
lines: kill the fat pig and salt it down for the winter

things: a fat pig of twenty stone
outcome: Killing, scalding, scraping and cutting up is a full day for three people, and the offal must be eaten or given away within days. The sides and hams take a stone of salt each, rubbed in hard and renewed over three to four weeks, and then they keep all winter. But curing is a race between the salt working inward and the meat going off from the bone outward, and warm weather tips it: in this mild spell the thin flitches cure sound, while one thick ham taints at the bone before the salt gets there. It looks and smells fine outside; a skewer run in to the bone a fortnight later comes out stinking. That ham is lost, and the flies have blown a corner of another.

outcome: A pair of rats gnaw up through a floorboard and have the loft to themselves, since the cat cannot get in. Each rat eats only an ounce or so a day, so the farmer notices nothing for a month; by spring a fifth of the grain is eaten or spilled, more is musty with urine, several sacks are useless as sacks, and the seed corn from fouled sacks comes up thin.

outcome: The hens put themselves to roost at dusk as always; nobody slides the board. The vixen, who tries this yard most nights, finds the hole open some time after midnight. In the panic inside she kills far more than she can carry: eleven hens bitten through the neck, one taken away, a second fetched and buried in the orchard. The dog barks at the noise, but chained and used to barking at nothing, he is ignored. The morning finds three live hens up in the rafters, too shocked to lay for a fortnight, and a drift of feathers. Eggs for the house and for market are gone until pullets are raised, which is five months.

outcome: The job takes a morning. The ground is stony and the player gets the hole knee deep instead of the thigh deep a post needs, rams the earth back as well as they can, and nails the rails on. It looks right and it turns the sheep, which only ever test a fence with their noses. But a cow uses a fence post to scratch on, leaning half a ton into it, and a shallow post in freshly dug earth rocks a little more each day. After a week of rain it lies over, the rails spring their nails, and the cattle are in the neighbour's wheat by morning. The green ash would also have rotted at the ground within three years.

place: A ten-acre wheat field at harvest, the crop cut and bound and standing in stooks of eight sheaves, waiting for a week of wind to dry before carting.
things: a week of warm drizzle and still air

outcome: Stooks shed a shower well enough, but a week of warm wet with no wind soaks them through. By the fourth day the grain in the ears, especially in the butts and on the sheltered side, begins to sprout, and sprouted wheat makes sticky, sweetish flour that will not bake a proper loaf. The bands rot, the sheaves slump, and birds work over the fallen ones. When a dry day comes every stook must be pulled apart and reset by hand, sheaf by sheaf, to air the insides, a day's work for three, and carting waits again. Perhaps a quarter of the crop is lost or fit only for the pigs, and the damp-carted rest needs watching in the stack.

place: A barn threshing floor of beaten clay between two big doors, on a still, foggy winter morning.

things: a flail, ash handstaff and holly swingle joined by a leather thong

outcome: Flailing is steady hard work: a practised hand threshes two dozen sheaves in a morning for about a bushel and a half of grain, and an unpractised one raps their own head with the swingle first. The result is grain mixed with as much chaff again by bulk. Winnowing needs moving air, a breeze through both doors that carries chaff aside while grain drops straight, and today there is none. Tossed in still air it all comes down together. Fanning with the basket works after a fashion, slowly and dustily: after an hour the grain is half clean, enough for the hens or a coarse grist, not for the miller. Proper cleaning waits for a windy day.

place: A field gateway after three days of rain, the ground poached to deep mud by cattle, on the only way from the root field to the yard.

outcome: On the firm headland the horse handles the full load. In the gateway the narrow wheels cut straight down to the hubs and the cart stops dead. Whipping the horse makes it plunge and strain, which digs its own feet in, risks a broken trace or a strained shoulder, and moves the cart not at all. What works is dull: tip or throw off half the load into the mud, lay brushwood in front of the wheels, let the horse take it out quietly, then come back for the rest in two more trips. An hour lost, the turnips from the mud filthy, and the gateway worse for the next load. A sensible carter would have taken half loads from the start.

place: A kitchen garden beside the yard in spring, rows of cabbage and lettuce seedlings a finger tall, and a henhouse that has just been cleaned out.

outcome: Meant as a kindness, it kills them. Fresh hen dung is fierce stuff: laid thick against young stems and watered in, it scorches the roots, and within three or four days the seedlings yellow from the edges, go limp and brown, and most die. The ones at the row ends, which got least, survive and later grow enormous. The same dung heaped for six months and turned would have been mild and rich, and the old black heap at the end of the yard was there for the taking. The bed is too strong to resow for some weeks, and is first-rate by midsummer. The smell brings flies for a week.

place: A farmyard with a stone-lined well five fathoms deep, in the eighth week without rain of a hot summer, with twelve cattle, two horses and a household to water from it.

outcome: The stock alone drink a hundred buckets a day in this heat. Week by week the water stands lower: first the rope has to be lengthened with a knotted piece, then the bucket comes up half full, then it comes up with silt in it because it is scraping the bottom. The well is not dry, it refills overnight to a few feet, but it gives perhaps thirty buckets a day when a hundred are wanted. So the cattle must be walked to the far pond morning and evening, losing condition and milk on the way, the household water is cloudy and must stand to settle, and the garden gets nothing. The first real rain does not mend it: the well takes weeks to recover after the ground has drunk its fill.

outcome: The cob has watched the latch lifted a thousand times and works it with his lip. He noses the lid off the bin and eats until he cannot, fifteen or twenty pounds of grain where his ration is four, then drinks deep at the trough. At dawn he looks merely full and rather pleased. By midday he is dull, off his feed and blowing; by evening he is pawing, looking at his flanks and wanting to roll with colic, and must be walked for hours to stop him twisting a gut. If he comes through that, two days later he stands rocked back on his heels with hot feet, foundered, and may never be fully sound. A peg through the latch would have stopped it.

outcome: A scythe cuts only while it is razor keen, and grass takes the edge off it in a few minutes. Freshly whetted and at dawn, with the dew making the grass stand heavy and cut sweet, the blade sings through and a good mower lays an acre in a day. Pushed on without whetting, it begins to bend the grass over and tear it, leaving a ragged ridge between strokes, and the work gets twice as hard for half the result. Whetting every five or ten minutes feels like lost time and is not. By mid-morning the dry grass is tough and the mowing slows regardless. A molehill dulls the edge at once; the hidden stone puts a nick in it that must be hammered out at home.

place: A sloping home field in early spring, the ewes brought close to the house for lambing, on a night of sleet driven by an east wind.
things: a hurdle and straw shelter in the field corner that the ewe does not use

outcome: The ewe lambs in the open on the windward slope, as ewes will. She licks the first lamb dry and it is up and sucking within half an hour. The second, born twenty minutes later while she is busy with the first, gets a few licks, stays wet, and in sleet a wet newborn chills past the point of standing within the hour. The shepherd's round finds it flat and cold-mouthed but alive. Rubbed with a sack, laid by the hearth and given a little warm first milk, it is on its feet by dawn; the hard part is then getting the ewe to take it back, and she may not, since it smells of kitchen now. Found an hour later it would have been dead, and the crow would have had its eyes at first light.

place: A farmhouse dairy with a plunger churn, on a frosty morning with the cream crock standing on a stone shelf as cold as the room.
lines: pour the cream into the churn and churn it into butter
keep churning

things: three days' cream, ripened and slightly sour, very cold
cold well water for washing the butter
outcome: Cream comes to butter in half an hour at the warmth of a mild spring day. Stone cold, it only froths and swells in the churn, and the player can plunge for two hours with aching arms and get nothing but foam. Setting the churn near the kitchen fire for a while, or standing the crock in warm water beforehand, fixes it and the butter comes in twenty minutes. The quick remedy of pouring hot water straight in overshoots: the butter comes at once but as a pale, greasy, soft mass that will not firm, keeps badly and tastes oily. Even good butter must be washed in cold water until it runs clear and worked with salt, or the trapped buttermilk turns it rancid within the week.
